name: Negation Pattern
description: Examines how the text expresses denial, contradiction, or absence (e.g., 'not', 'never', 'un-', 'non-'). AI models heavily favor simple, direct analytic negation ('do not', 'is not') and struggle to authentically generate complex, double, or subtle morphological negations that human writers use for rhetorical nuance.
algorithm: Syntactic and Morphological Negation Distribution Analysis
mechanism: This method parses the text to identify all instances of negation, mapping them into three categories: analytic (explicitly using 'not' or 'no'), morphological (using prefixes/suffixes like 'un-', 'im-', '-less'), and inherent (words carrying negative semantic weight like 'deny', 'refuse', 'fail'). Large Language Models (LLMs) are statistically trained to maximize clarity and avoid logical ambiguity. Consequently, they predominantly rely on the safest, most statistically common form of negation: simple analytic negation (e.g., 'It is not easy' rather than 'It is uneasy' or 'It is far from simple'). AI consistently avoids double negations ('not uncommon') or complex scope negation where the negative marker applies to a distant clause, as these increase computational uncertainty during generation. Human writers naturally employ a rich spectrum of negations, often using morphological prefixes or inherent negative verbs to convey subtle degrees of contradiction or irony. An unnatural over-reliance on simple 'not/no' constructs strongly indicates an AI prioritizing safe, explicit statistical generation over stylistic variance.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing persuasive essays, literature reviews, and opinion pieces, distinguishing the rich, nuanced contradictions of a human author from the straightforward, mathematically 'safe' denials of an AI.
strengths:
• Targets a deep statistical bias in autoregressive models that structural RLHF alignment actually reinforces (the drive for maximum clarity).
• Highly effective even on relatively short texts, as negation is a frequent and necessary part of all discourse.
• Difficult to bypass via simple prompt engineering without making the resulting text sound bizarrely unnatural.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives when analyzing texts written by non-native speakers, language learners, or technical manuals, which inherently favor simple analytic negation for clarity.
• Less effective if the human writer has a deliberately simple, Hemingway-esque writing style.
• Cannot distinguish between simple human writing and AI writing if the target genre strictly mandates plain language.
parameters:
Analysis: Dependency Parsing and Negation Scope Mapping
Metric: Ratio of Analytic vs. Morphological/Inherent Negation
Output: 0-100 Negation Simplicity (Statistical Safety) Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 72-80% accuracy. Strongest when analyzing academic, creative, or argumentative texts where complex negation is structurally expected.

references.title: Manning, C.D. & Schütze, H. (1999). Foundations of Statistical Natural Language Processing. MIT Press.
Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
